Scope and preparation

写二阶行列式定义。解方程公式只简述，不再写消元和代回过程。

Good morning. Today we will study determinants. We will focus on definitions, theorems, and proofs. First, we will study permutations. Then we will define the determinant of order n. Finally, we will prove that a matrix and its transpose have the same determinant.
Definition (determinant of order two). The determinant of a two-by-two matrix is the product of its main-diagonal entries minus the product of its other two entries.

This formula defines the determinant of order two. We use it to solve a system of two linear equations in two unknowns. Let A be the coefficient matrix. Suppose its determinant is not zero. To find each unknown, replace its column in A with the right-hand side of the system. Take the determinant of this new matrix. Then divide it by the determinant of A. This is Cramer's rule for two unknowns. The textbook proves the rule for n unknowns later.

For a determinant of higher order, we need to answer two questions. Which products do we use? Which products get a plus sign, and which get a minus sign? To answer these questions, we first need permutations.

title: Permutations and parity
zh: 定义1—3 排列、逆序与奇偶性

blocks.text: Definition 1 (permutation). A permutation of order n is an arrangement of the numbers 1 to n in which each number appears exactly once. The arrangement 1, 2, ..., n is called the natural order.

Let us begin with the definition of a permutation. Take the numbers from one to n. Put them in an order. Use each number exactly once. This is a permutation of order n. There are n choices for the first place. There are n minus one choices for the second place. We continue in this way. So there are n factorial permutations. The order one, two, up to n is called the natural order.
Definition 2 (inversion and inversion number). An inversion is a pair of entries in which the larger entry comes before the smaller one. The inversion number is the total number of such pairs.

Look at two entries in a permutation. If the larger entry comes first, the pair is an inversion. The two entries do not have to be next to each other. Count all such pairs. The total is the inversion number. We use the letter tau for this number.
只完整计算2431这一例，指明(2,1)并不相邻。

Look at two, four, three, one. The inversions are two and one, four and three, four and one, and three and one. There are four inversions. Here is an easy way to count them. For each entry, count the smaller entries to its right. Then add these numbers. This counts each inversion once.
Definition 3 (even and odd permutations). A permutation is even if its inversion number is even, and odd if its inversion number is odd.

If the inversion number is even, we call the permutation even. If the inversion number is odd, we call the permutation odd. The word parity means being even or odd. Our example has four inversions, so it is even. The natural order has no inversions. Zero is even, so the natural order is even too. We can use the same definitions for any n distinct natural numbers. We only need to compare which number is larger.
Definition (transposition). A transposition exchanges two entries of a permutation and leaves all other entries fixed. It is adjacent if the two entries are next to each other.

Next, let us define a transposition. A transposition means swapping two entries. All other entries stay in place. For example, swap one and two in two, four, three, one. We get one, four, three, two. The two entries do not have to be next to each other. If they are next to each other, we call this an adjacent transposition.

If we swap the same two entries again, we get the original permutation back. Suppose n is at least two. Fix two positions and swap the entries in them. This puts all permutations into pairs. The two permutations in each pair are different, because all entries are distinct. We can now ask how a transposition changes the parity.
保留“对换做两次恢复原状”，随后推论使用它证明配对是一一对应。
Theorem 1. A transposition changes the parity of a permutation: an even permutation becomes odd, and an odd permutation becomes even.
We now come to Theorem One. A transposition changes the parity of a permutation. An even permutation becomes odd, and an odd permutation becomes even. Let us prove this in two cases.
Two entries next to each other

First, suppose j and k are next to each other. Every other entry is either before both of them or after both of them. After the transposition, this is still true. So its inversion pairs with j and k do not change. Pairs that contain neither j nor k do not change either.

Only the pair j, k changes. If j is greater than k, we lose one inversion. If j is less than k, we gain one inversion. So the inversion number changes by one. An even number becomes odd, and an odd number becomes even.
Any two entries
Now suppose there are s entries between j and k. We can swap j and k by a series of adjacent transpositions, as shown here. This takes two s plus one transpositions in total.
After these transpositions, only j and k have changed places. All other entries are back in their original positions.
As we proved above, each adjacent transposition changes the parity. Two s plus one is odd. So after these transpositions, the parity changes. This completes the proof.
指向板书中的两阶段交换过程，简述总共需要2s+1次相邻对换；指出其他元素回到原位置，再用奇数次奇偶性改变结束证明。
Corollary. For n at least 2, the numbers of even and odd permutations of order n are equal. Each is n factorial divided by 2.
Next, let us introduce a corollary of Theorem One. Suppose n is at least two. Then the number of odd permutations equals the number of even permutations. Each number is n factorial divided by two.

Now let us prove this corollary. Let s be the number of odd permutations. Let t be the number of even permutations. Take each odd permutation and swap its first two entries. This is a transposition. By Theorem One, the new permutation is even.

Different odd permutations give different even permutations. Why? If two results were the same, we could swap the first two entries again. We would get the same original permutation. So we get s different even permutations. This means s is at most t. Now start with the even permutations and do the same thing. We get t at most s. Therefore, s equals t.

There are n factorial permutations in total. Half are odd, and half are even. So each number is n factorial divided by two. We need n to be at least two. When n is one, there is only one permutation, and it is even.

Theorem 2. Every permutation can be changed into natural order by a finite sequence of transpositions, and conversely. Every such sequence has an even number of transpositions for an even permutation and an odd number for an odd permutation.

Next, we come to Theorem Two. It says that we can put any permutation into natural order by a series of transpositions. We can also go back from natural order to that permutation. The number of transpositions is even for an even permutation. It is odd for an odd permutation. First, we prove that we can put the entries in order. Then we prove the statement about the number of transpositions.
Putting the entries in order

We use induction on n. When n is one, the permutation is already in natural order. We need no transpositions. Now assume we can sort every permutation of order n minus one. Let us consider a permutation of order n.
First, suppose the last entry is n. The first n minus one entries are the numbers from one to n minus one. By our assumption, we can put these entries in order. We leave the last entry, n, in place.

If the last entry is not n, swap it with n. Now n is in the last place. We can use the previous case to sort the other entries. This completes the induction. To go back, do the same transpositions in reverse order. This takes us from natural order to the original permutation.

blocks.text: Is the number of transpositions even or odd?

The natural order is even. Start from it and make m transpositions. Each transposition changes the parity. If m is even, the final permutation is even. If m is odd, the final permutation is odd. So m and the final inversion number are both even or both odd. Going back uses the same number of transpositions. This proves the statement in both directions.

We may sort the same permutation in different ways. The number of transpositions may change. But these numbers are always all even or all odd. We will use this fact to choose the signs in a determinant.

title: The determinant of order n
zh: 新增 定义4与符号规则

blocks.text: 新增内容。从这里起所有元素属于固定数域P。先写一般方阵，再写求和定义，口述说明下标。

Definition 4 (determinant of order n). Choose exactly one entry from each row and each column, and write their product in increasing row order. Give it a plus sign if the column permutation is even and a minus sign if it is odd. The determinant is the sum of these signed products over all column permutations.

We now have the facts about permutations that we need. Let us use them to define the determinant of order n. From now on, all entries are in a fixed field P, a subfield of the complex numbers. We have n rows and n columns. To make one product, choose one entry from each row and each column. Multiply the chosen entries. We then give each product a plus or minus sign and add all the terms. This gives the determinant.
Write the factors in row order: row one first, row two next, and so on. The product has this form. The column numbers j one, j two, up to j n must form a permutation of one to n.

blocks.latex: a_{1j_1}a_{2j_2}\cdots a_{nj_n},\qquad j_1j_2\cdots j_n\text{ a permutation}

blocks.text: Here is Definition Four. If the column permutation is even, use a plus sign. If it is odd, use a minus sign. Do this for every column permutation, and add the terms.

Let us read the formula in parts. We sum over all column permutations. For each one, take minus one to the power of its inversion number. Then multiply by the chosen entries. There are n factorial terms before we combine them. Some may be zero. Some may cancel each other. Addition, subtraction, and multiplication keep us in P. So the determinant is also in P.

For order two, the column permutations are one, two and two, one. Their inversion numbers are zero and one. So we get the formula we already know. For order three, there are six permutations. They give the six terms shown here.
Remember the rule. First, write the factors in row order. Then use the column permutation to find the sign. Soon we will see how to find the sign when the factors are in any order.

title: Some useful determinants
zh: 新增 例题与三角行列式证明

blocks.text: A short example

Let us use this definition in a few examples. In this example, every row has only one nonzero entry. Only one product can be nonzero. Its column order is four, three, two, one. This has six inversions, so we use a plus sign. The product is one times two times three times four. The determinant is twenty-four.
Upper triangular determinants
Definition (upper triangular matrix). A square matrix is upper triangular if every entry below its main diagonal is zero.
Result (upper triangular determinant). The determinant of an upper triangular matrix equals the product of its diagonal entries.

For an upper triangular matrix, all entries below the main diagonal are zero. Let us use the definition to find its determinant. Consider a product that is not zero. In the last row, we must choose a sub n n. Every other entry in that row is zero. So j sub n equals n.

Now look at row n minus one. Only the last two columns can have nonzero entries. We have already used column n. We cannot use it again. So we must choose column n minus one. Continue upwards, one row at a time. In every row, we must choose the diagonal entry.

So all other terms are zero. Only the diagonal product can remain. Its column order is one, two, up to n. This is even, so its sign is plus. This proves the formula. If a diagonal entry is zero, the diagonal product is zero too. The formula still holds.

Definition (main diagonal and diagonal matrix). The main diagonal consists of the entries whose row and column indices are equal. A diagonal matrix is a square matrix whose entries outside this diagonal are all zero.
Corollary (diagonal determinant). The determinant of a diagonal matrix equals the product of its diagonal entries. In particular, the identity matrix has determinant 1.

The main diagonal goes from the top left to the bottom right. In a diagonal matrix, every entry outside this diagonal is zero. A diagonal matrix is also upper triangular. So its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries. For the identity matrix, these entries are all one. Its determinant is therefore one.

title: The sign of a term in any order
zh: 新增 一般项符号及完整证明

blocks.text: Result (sign of a determinant term). Write a product that contains exactly one entry from each row and each column in any order. Its coefficient in the determinant formula is plus 1 if the sum of the row and column inversion numbers is even, and minus 1 if that sum is odd.

Next, let us find the sign when the factors are written in any order. We can change the order of factors without changing their product. Now write a determinant product in any order, as shown here. The row indices form a permutation. The column indices also form a permutation.

To find the sign, count the inversions in the row indices. Then count them in the column indices. Add the two numbers. If the sum is even, use plus. If it is odd, use minus. Here we mean the sign placed before the product in the determinant formula. We do not mean whether the product itself is a positive or negative number.
Proof

Let us prove this rule. Swap factors until the row indices are in natural order. We can do this by Theorem Two. Call the new column indices j prime one, up to j prime n. Now the product is in the row order used in the definition.

When we swap two factors, we swap two row indices and two column indices at the same time. This gives one transposition in each sequence. By Theorem One, each inversion number changes from even to odd or from odd to even. Both change parity. So their sum stays even or stays odd.

At the end, the row indices are in natural order. Their inversion number is zero. So our sign formula now uses only the inversion number of the new column order. This is exactly the sign in the definition. The sum kept the same parity at every step. So the formula gives the correct sign in the original order too. This proves the rule.
A sign check
保留教材这一例，它直接检验新公式；不新增额外计算练习。

In this example, the row indices are two, three, one, four. They have two inversions. The column indices are one, two, four, three. They have one inversion. The sum is three, so we use a minus sign. To check, put the factors in row order. The column order becomes four, one, two, three. This has three inversions and gives the same minus sign.

title: A matrix and its transpose have the same determinant
zh: 新增 按列定义与性质1证明

blocks.text: Writing the definition in column order
Result (column-order formula). The determinant can also be written with the factors in increasing column order. In this form, the sign of each term is determined by the parity of its row permutation.

We can now use this sign rule to write the determinant in column order. In the sign formula, we add the row inversion number and the column inversion number. We can put the factors in column order instead of row order. Then the column inversion number is zero. Only the row inversion number determines the sign.
This formula gives the same determinant. We still choose one entry from each row and each column. We only change how we write the factors. Here, column one comes first, then column two, and so on.
Property 1 and proof
Definition (transpose). The transpose of a matrix is obtained by turning its rows into columns. The entry in row i, column j becomes the entry in row j, column i.
Property 1. A square matrix and its transpose have the same determinant.

To transpose a matrix, change its rows into columns. The entry in row i, column j moves to row j, column i. Property One says that this does not change the determinant. Let A be the original matrix. Let B be its transpose.

Let us prove this. Write the determinant of B in column order. Since B is the transpose of A, b sub i k equals a sub k i. Replace each entry of B in the sum with the matching entry of A. Now we have exactly the definition of the determinant of A in row order.

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}\det B&=\sum_{i_1\cdots i_n}(-1)^{\tau(i_1\cdots i_n)}b_{i_1 1}\cdots b_{i_n n}\\&=\sum_{i_1\cdots i_n}(-1)^{\tau(i_1\cdots i_n)}a_{1i_1}\cdots a_{ni_n}\\&=\det A.\end{aligned}

blocks.text: So A and its transpose have the same determinant. This proves Property One. Here, we change all rows into columns. This is a different operation from swapping two entries in a permutation.
The lower triangular case
Definition (lower triangular matrix). A square matrix is lower triangular if every entry above its main diagonal is zero.
Corollary (lower triangular determinant). The determinant of a lower triangular matrix equals the product of its diagonal entries.

In a lower triangular matrix, all entries above the main diagonal are zero. Its transpose is upper triangular. The diagonal entries stay the same. We know the determinant does not change under transpose. We also know the formula for an upper triangular matrix. So the lower triangular determinant is the product of its diagonal entries too.
We can use transpose to turn a result about rows into a result about columns. We will use this idea again in the next section.

Let us review. First, we used inversions to define even and odd permutations. We proved that one transposition changes the parity. Next, we used permutations to define the determinant. Each product uses one entry from each row and each column. The permutation tells us which sign to use. For a triangular matrix, the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries. We then found the sign when the factors are in any order. Finally, we proved that a matrix and its transpose have the same determinant. Next time, we will study more properties of determinants. Thank you.

title: Formula reading guide
time: 备课参考 · 不额外占用课堂时间

blocks.text: 下面读法覆盖原有与新增内容。长公式先说明结构，再指向各部分，不必逐项机械朗读。
“a sub i j”; “a sub one, j one.” 指向板书，区分行指标1与列指标j₁。
“tau of the permutation j one through j n.”
“n factorial”; “n factorial divided by two.”
“minus one raised to the inversion number of the column permutation.”
“sum over all permutations j one through j n.”
“the product of a sub one j one through a sub n j n.”
“minus one raised to the sum of the inversion numbers of the row and column permutations.”
“m is congruent to tau modulo two”; in simple words, “m and the inversion number are both even or both odd.”
“A transpose”; “the determinant of A transpose equals the determinant of A.”
“b sub i j equals a sub j i.”
“j sub n minus one equals n minus one.” 第一个n−1整体是下标。
Terms for the added section
upper triangular determinant：上三角行列式；lower triangular determinant：下三角行列式；main diagonal：主对角线；transpose：转置；row index / column index：行指标／列指标；assigned sign：展开项前的正负号；commutativity of multiplication：乘法交换律。
transposition：对换（正式术语）；adjacent transposition：相邻对换；swap two entries：交换两个元素（描述动作）。陈述定理、引用结论和计算次数时使用 transposition；说明具体操作时可用动词 swap。
